q-147887.name: Question 1
q-147887.problem:
The disjoint union ${A}_{1}⊔{A}_{2}⊔{A}_{3}⊔{A}_{4}$ of events ${A}_{1},{A}_{2},{A}_{3},{A}_{4}$ covers the entire sample space. Compute $P({A}_{1}|B)$ given the following probabilities:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P(B|{A}_{1})=\frac{1}{5}, &  \\  & P(B|{A}_{2})=0, & P({A}_{2})=\frac{1}{4} \\  & P(B|{A}_{3})=\frac{1}{5}, & P({A}_{3})=\frac{1}{8} \\  & P(B|{A}_{4})=\frac{2}{5}, & P({A}_{4})=\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$
q-147887.worked_solution:
If the disjoint union ${A}_{1}⊔{A}_{2}⊔…⊔{A}_{n}$ covers the entire sample space, Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability gives us the following:

$$
P({A}_{k}|B)=\frac{P(B|{A}_{k})P({A}_{k})}{P(B)}=\frac{P(B|{A}_{k})P({A}_{k})}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}P(B|{A}_{i})P({A}_{i})}
$$

where $k=1,2,…,n.$

In our case, $n=4,$ and ${A}_{1}⊔{A}_{2}⊔{A}_{3}⊔{A}_{4}$ covers the entire sample space. Consequently, we have

$$
P({A}_{1})+P({A}_{2})+P({A}_{3})+P({A}_{4})=1.
$$

As a result,

$$
\begin{aligned}P({A}_{1}) & =1-(P({A}_{2})+P({A}_{3})+P({A}_{4})) \\  & =1-(\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{3}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P({A}_{1}|B) & =\frac{P(B|{A}_{1})P({A}_{1})}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{4}P(B|{A}_{i})P({A}_{i})} \\  & =\frac{P(B|{A}_{1})P({A}_{1})}{P(B|{A}_{1})P({A}_{1})+P(B|{A}_{2})P({A}_{2})+P(B|{A}_{3})P({A}_{3})+P(B|{A}_{4})P({A}_{4})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{5})(\frac{3}{8})}{(\frac{1}{5})(\frac{3}{8})+(0)(\frac{1}{4})+(\frac{1}{5})(\frac{1}{8})+(\frac{2}{5})(\frac{1}{4})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{40})}{(\frac{1}{5})} \\  & =\frac{3}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

P(B|A1)=15,P(B|A2)=0,P(A2)=14P(B|A3)=15,P(A3)=18P(B|A4)=25,P(A4)=14

If the disjoint union A1⊔A2⊔…⊔An covers the entire sample space, Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability gives us the following:

P(Ak|B)=P(B|Ak)P(Ak)P(B)=P(B|Ak)P(Ak)∑i=1nP(B|Ai)P(Ai)

where k=1,2,…,n.

In our case, n=4, and A1⊔A2⊔A3⊔A4 covers the entire sample space. Consequently, we have

P(A1)+P(A2)+P(A3)+P(A4)=1.

As a result,

P(A1)=1−(P(A2)+P(A3)+P(A4))=1−(14+18+14)=38.

Therefore,

P(A1|B)=P(B|A1)P(A1)∑i=14P(B|Ai)P(Ai)=P(B|A1)P(A1)P(B|A1)P(A1)+P(B|A2)P(A2)+P(B|A3)P(A3)+P(B|A4)P(A4)=(15)(38)(15)(38)+(0)(14)+(15)(18)+(25)(14)=(340)(15)=38.

$$
\begin{aligned} & P(B|{A}_{1})=\frac{1}{5}, & P({A}_{1})=\frac{1}{4} \\  & P(B|{A}_{2})=\frac{1}{8}, & P({A}_{2})=\frac{2}{5} \\  & P(B|{A}_{3})=1, & P({A}_{3})=\frac{7}{20}\end{aligned}
$$

If the disjoint union ${A}_{1}⊔{A}_{2}⊔…⊔{A}_{n}$ covers the entire sample space, Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability gives us the following:

$$

$$

In our case, $n=3,$ and ${A}_{1}⊔{A}_{2}⊔{A}_{3}$ covers the entire sample space. Consequently, we have

$$
P({A}_{1})+P({A}_{2})+P({A}_{3})=\frac{1}{4}+\frac{2}{5}+\frac{7}{20}=1.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P({A}_{2}|B) & =\frac{P(B|{A}_{2})P({A}_{2})}{{\sum }_{i=1}^{3}P(B|{A}_{i})P({A}_{i})} \\  & =\frac{P(B|{A}_{2})P({A}_{2})}{P(B|{A}_{1})P({A}_{1})+P(B|{A}_{2})P({A}_{2})+P(B|{A}_{3})P({A}_{3})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{8})(\frac{2}{5})}{(\frac{1}{5})(\frac{1}{4})+(\frac{1}{8})(\frac{2}{5})+(1)(\frac{7}{20})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{20})}{(\frac{9}{20})} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}

q-148673.name: Question 6
q-148673.problem:
Arthur and Sara are finding the best recipe for chocolate muffins, and they test three different oven cooking modes, mode $1,$ mode $2,$ and mode $3.$ They also try two types of yeast, A and B.

- They use mode $1$ to cook the $30%$ of their muffins, and $90%$ of those muffins turn out well.

- They use mode $2$ to cook the $40%$ of their muffins, and $85%$ of those muffins turn out well.

- They use mode $3$ to cook the $30%$ of their muffins, and $88%$ of those muffins turn out well.

If $20%$ of all muffins was prepared with yeast A, and $87%$ of yeast A muffins turn out well, what is the probability that a randomly chosen good muffin is done with yeast A? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
q-148673.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the event that a muffin is made with yeast A, $G$ be the event that a muffin turns out well, and ${M}_{1},{M}_{2},{M}_{3}$ be the event that a muffin is cooked with mode $1,$ $2,$ or $3,$ respectively. 

Let's break down the information given in the problem statement:

- From the bullet points, we have the following information:

$$
\begin{aligned} & P({M}_{1})=0.3 &  & P(G|{M}_{1})=0.9 \\  & P({M}_{2})=0.4 &  & P(G|{M}_{2})=0.85 \\  & P({M}_{3})=0.3 &  & P(G|{M}_{3})=0.88\end{aligned}
$$

The disjoint union ${M}_{1}⊔{M}_{2}⊔{M}_{3}$ covers the entire sample space, and we have

$$
P({M}_{1})+P({M}_{2})+P({M}_{3})=0.3+0.4+0.3=1.
$$

- Since $20%$ of muffins are made with yeast A, we have

$$
P(A)=0.2.
$$

- Since $87%$ of muffins made with yeast A turn out well, we have

$$
P(G|A)=0.87.
$$

We want to find the probability that a randomly chosen good muffin is made with yeast A, which is represented as $P(A|G).$ 

Using Bayes' theorem combined with the law of total probability, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(A|G) & =\frac{P(G|A)P(A)}{P(G)} \\  & =\frac{P(G|A)P(A)}{P(G|{M}_{1})P({M}_{1})+P(G|{M}_{2})P({M}_{2})+P(G|{M}_{3})P({M}_{3})} \\  & =\frac{(0.87)(0.2)}{(0.9)(0.3)+(0.85)(0.4)+(0.88)(0.3)} \\  & =\frac{0.174}{0.874} \\  & ≈0.199,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

$$

$$

$$
P({T}_{1})+P({T}_{2})+P({T}_{3})=0.44+0.32+0.24=1.

$$

$$
